client: I started this new job in marketing about six weeks ago, and honestly, I feel like I'm drowning most days. Everyone around me seems so confident and experienced, and I keep worrying that I'm way behind where I should be. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like these first six weeks have been really overwhelming — that feeling of looking around and thinking everyone else has it figured out while you're just trying to keep your head above water is exhausting and isolating. I also notice that even reaching out today took some courage, and there's a part of you that's not sure it'll help, which makes sense when you're already feeling stretched thin. What would feel like the most important thing to start with — the worry about being "behind," or that sense that talking might not make a difference?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think the worry about being behind is probably the bigger thing, honestly, because it's with me basically every single day at work. Like, I'll be in a meeting and someone will throw out some industry term or reference a campaign strategy I've never heard of, and I just freeze up inside, terrified someone's going to notice I have no idea what they're talking about. It's gotten to the point where I'm second-guessing even the small decisions, which makes everything take twice as long.
therapist: That daily dread of being "found out" — especially in those meeting moments where you freeze — sounds genuinely exhausting to carry around, and it makes sense it's spilling over into even the smaller decisions. What you're describing is something we call the impostor experience, where your brain is essentially working overtime to scan for threats, which actually makes it *harder* to access what you do know. I'm curious — when you freeze in those moments, what's the story your mind is telling you about what it would mean if someone *did* notice?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think the story is something like, if they notice, they'll realize hiring me was a mistake, and it's only a matter of time before they let me go. And underneath that there's this other layer where I feel like I should already know all of this, like I'm somehow failing at something everyone else manages to do just fine. It's almost like I'm waiting for the moment it all falls apart, which I know sounds dramatic, but it feels very real.
therapist: What you're describing doesn't sound dramatic at all — it sounds like a mind that's been working incredibly hard to brace for something painful, and that kind of constant vigilance is genuinely wearing. I notice as you said that, there was something almost quiet and rushed about it, like maybe these thoughts feel a little vulnerable or even shameful to say out loud. I want to gently ask — this belief that you *should* already know everything at six weeks in, where do you think that standard comes from, and would you apply it to someone else starting a new role?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, when you put it that way, no, I wouldn't expect someone else to walk into a new job and know everything after six weeks, that would be ridiculous. But for some reason the rule feels different when it applies to me, like I have to prove I deserve to be there in a way other people don't. I think some of it probably comes from growing up always needing to be on top of things to feel okay, but I'm not sure recognizing that actually makes the feeling go away.
therapist: You've just made a really important connection — that this double standard has roots that go back further than this job, which takes genuine self-awareness to see. And you're right that insight alone doesn't flip a switch on the feeling, but it does give us something to work with, because we can start to gently challenge that older rule rather than just accepting it as truth. I'm wondering — when you imagine the version of you that *does* deserve to be there without having to prove it constantly, what would that actually look like day to day?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, I find it hard to even picture that version of me, because the constant checking and proving feels so built in that I'm not sure what would be left without it. I guess maybe it would look like sitting in a meeting and not knowing something and just... asking, without the panic spiral that follows. But even imagining that makes me anxious, because what if letting my guard down is exactly when things go wrong?
therapist: That image you described — just asking a question in a meeting without the spiral — is actually a really meaningful one, and the fact that it makes you anxious tells us something important: part of you has learned that staying vigilant is what keeps you safe, so relaxing it feels like risk rather than relief. It's worth gently questioning that assumption though — has the constant checking and proving actually prevented anything from going wrong, or has it mostly just cost you a lot of energy? I'm curious what evidence you have, from this job or others, that letting your guard down even slightly has ever actually led to the disaster your mind is predicting.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: When I actually think about it, I can't really point to a specific time where letting my guard down caused some disaster, and the vigilance hasn't stopped me from feeling terrified anyway, so I guess it's not exactly working as advertised. But I think my mind immediately goes to, well, maybe it's been preventing things I just don't know about, like the anxiety is secretly doing its job behind the scenes. It's a hard thing to argue against because the absence of disaster feels like proof it's working, even when logically I can see that's a bit circular.
therapist: You've just identified something really sophisticated — that unfalsifiable loop where the anxiety takes credit for every okay outcome, which makes it almost impossible to challenge from the inside. I notice there's something a little tentative in how you're saying all this, like you can see the logic clearly but it doesn't quite land with full conviction yet, which makes sense because we're up against a belief that's been protecting you for a long time. What do you think it would take — even a small experiment — to start gathering some real evidence about what actually happens when you ease up on the vigilance just slightly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think the most manageable experiment would be asking a question in a meeting when I genuinely don't know something, instead of staying quiet and spiraling afterward trying to figure it out on my own. But I'm already anticipating the problem with that, which is that in the moment, the fear of looking incompetent is so loud that I'm not sure I'll actually be able to override it just because we talked about this here. It feels a bit like knowing you should jump into cold water doesn't make it any less cold when you're standing at the edge.
therapist: That cold water analogy is really apt, and it tells me you understand yourself well — knowing something intellectually and feeling safe enough to do it are two very different things, and that gap is exactly where we'd want to focus. One thing that can help is making the experiment as small as possible, so instead of framing it as "overriding the fear," it becomes just noticing what actually happens after you ask — does the disaster your mind predicted show up, or something else? Would it help to think through what a genuinely low-stakes version of that question might look like, so the edge of the pool feels a little less high before you jump?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Yeah, I think breaking it down like that does make it feel slightly less impossible, like maybe I could ask something in a smaller team setting rather than in front of the whole department. But I'm a little worried that I'll go into work tomorrow and the moment will come and I'll just freeze and then feel worse about myself for not following through, which would kind of confirm the story that I can't do this. I guess I'm wondering how you're supposed to actually build confidence when every attempt feels like it could just become more evidence against you.
therapist: The way you just described that — quickly, like the worry was tumbling out faster than you could catch it — makes me think this fear of "failing the experiment" might actually feel more urgent than the original challenge of asking the question. What you've landed on is a really important CBT insight though: confidence doesn't come *before* the attempt, it's built from surviving the attempt, including the imperfect ones — so even freezing tomorrow wouldn't be evidence you can't do this, it would just be data about what made it hard that time. What if we agreed that whatever happens tomorrow, you'd try to look at it with the same curiosity you'd offer a colleague, rather than as a verdict on whether you belong there?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I like the idea of treating it as data rather than a verdict, and part of me genuinely wants to believe that framing would hold up in the moment. But I think my honest worry is that I'm much kinder to other people than I am to myself, so that curiosity you're describing might just not be available to me when I'm standing in the middle of it feeling embarrassed. It's like I know the right answer here in this room, but I'm not sure that version of me comes to work with me tomorrow.
therapist: The way you said that — quietly, almost like you were confiding something you weren't sure you were allowed to say — really landed, and I think you've named something really honest and important: that self-compassion feels genuinely less accessible to you than it does when you're thinking about someone else. That gap *is* the work, and it didn't appear overnight, so it won't close overnight either — but the fact that you can already see the kinder framework, even if you can't fully inhabit it yet, means it's not completely out of reach. I'm wondering, is there anyone in your life — a friend, a mentor — whose voice you *can* hear in those hard moments, someone whose perspective on you feels a little more trustworthy than your own right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: There's maybe one person, my friend Cara, who's known me for a long time and tends to see me more generously than I see myself, and I think if she were in that meeting she'd probably say something like, of course you don't know everything yet, you've been there six weeks. But I'm not sure I can actually summon her voice in the moment, it feels a bit artificial, like I'd be play-acting at believing something I don't really believe. I guess I'm also a little embarrassed to admit that I need to borrow someone else's perspective just to get through a work meeting.
therapist: The embarrassment you just named — about needing Cara's voice — is actually worth pausing on, because borrowing a kinder perspective isn't a weakness or pretending, it's how we all internalize new ways of seeing ourselves over time, and you've been running on that harsh inner voice for so long that a gentler one genuinely needs practice to feel real. And Cara's words — "of course you don't know everything yet, you've been there six weeks" — aren't artificial just because they feel unfamiliar; they're actually just accurate. What do you think it says about you that someone who knows you well, really well, sees you that generously?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
